summary: Polkadot/Substrate accounts support three separate signature schemes: sr25519 (Schnorrkel — Schnorr signatures over Ristretto-compressed Curve25519, the default), Ed25519, and ECDSA over secp256k1 — the official wiki is explicit these are three distinct options, not curve variants of one scheme. sr25519 is dual-purpose like Solana's Ed25519: the same keys back BABE block-production consensus, which needs a verifiable random function for slot-leader election as well as ordinary signing — sr25519 provides both. sr25519 also supports native key aggregation and hierarchical derivation (HDKD) that plain Ed25519 lacks.
no_protocol_reason: Polkadot's account signing and BABE consensus are chain-specific mechanisms, not standardised network protocols tracked by the matrix.

summary: CometBFT, the consensus engine underlying the Cosmos Hub and every Cosmos SDK chain, signs validator votes/precommits with Ed25519 — 'currently CometBFT uses Ed25519 keys which are widely supported across the security sector and HSMs.' Cosmos SDK v0.55.0 (2026-07-27) shipped real, opt-in ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) support for BOTH validator consensus keys and user account keys — mnemonic keyring creation, transaction signing/verification, multisig, and genesis key-rotation support, all PR-linked in the release changelog. This is a meaningfully stronger PQC story than most chains: real, shipped, testable code rather than a proposal or a research roadmap — but chains built on the SDK still default to Ed25519-only consensus keys in genesis, so no production chain has adopted it yet.
no_protocol_reason: Cosmos consensus signing is a chain-specific mechanism (CometBFT), not a standardised network protocol tracked by the matrix.

summary: Avalanche's virtual machine uses secp256k1 ECDSA for transaction signing; X-Chain and P-Chain addresses hash the ECDSA public key, following the same approach as Bitcoin. No post-quantum work was found for this specific mechanism.

summary: Avalanche Interchain Messaging (ICM, formerly Avalanche Warp Messaging) uses BLS signatures for cross-subnet message attestation: every validator holds a BLS key pair, and signatures from a threshold of the source subnet's stake are combined into a single aggregated BLS multi-signature — a genuine cryptographic threshold signature, unlike the plain N-independent-signature multisig Wormhole and Safe use for the same class of problem.

summary: Arbitrum's AnyTrust L2s (a lower-cost variant of Nitro rollups) rely on a Data Availability Committee rather than posting full data to Ethereum L1. Each committee member signs a (data hash, expiry) pair with a BLS key; once enough members respond, the sequencer aggregates the signatures into a single BLS12-381 aggregated signature (a DACert) posted to the L1 inbox contract — the same underlying curve as Ethereum's own consensus-layer BLS, and, like Avalanche's interchain messaging, a genuine aggregated threshold signature rather than a plain N-signature multisig. Base transaction signing on both Arbitrum and Optimism is inherited, unmodified Ethereum secp256k1 ECDSA — Optimism's own sequencer and its permissionless Fault Proof dispute system have no comparably distinct signature mechanism of their own, so neither warrants a separate row here.
no_protocol_reason: Arbitrum AnyTrust's data-availability attestation is a chain-specific protocol, not a standardised network protocol tracked by the matrix.
